topic.subject: social
topic.title: Minerals and energy resources
topic.scope: ferrous and non-ferrous minerals, mining, conventional and non-conventional energy, conservation of energy

misconceptions.why: Students often associate the word 'metal' with 'iron' due to its common usage.
misconceptions.fix: Ferrous minerals contain iron, while non-ferrous minerals like copper or gold do not contain iron.

probe.question: Is gold a ferrous mineral?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a metal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a category name implies all its members are identical

misconceptions.statement: Mining is only done by digging deep vertical shafts.
misconceptions.why: Visuals of mining in media often focus on deep underground shafts.
misconceptions.fix: Mining can be open-cast (surface), shaft (deep underground), or drilling, depending on the depth of the mineral deposit.

probe.question: How is coal extracted if it is near the surface?

misconceptions.root_belief: one specific example represents the entire process

misconceptions.statement: Coal is a renewable resource because we keep finding more.
misconceptions.why: Confusing the rate of discovery with the rate of geological formation.
misconceptions.fix: Coal is a non-renewable resource because it takes millions of years to form and cannot be replaced once consumed.

probe.question: Will we run out of coal?
probe.wrong_answer: No, we keep finding new mines.

misconceptions.statement: Non-conventional energy is always more efficient than conventional energy.
misconceptions.why: Marketing and media hype around 'green' energy often ignore efficiency and scale constraints.
misconceptions.fix: Non-conventional energy is sustainable, but its efficiency and reliability depend on technology and environmental conditions.

probe.question: Is solar energy always better than coal?

misconceptions.root_belief: new is always better than old

misconceptions.statement: Metallic minerals are always hard and non-metallic minerals are always soft.
misconceptions.why: Students link 'metal' with strength and 'non-metal' with brittleness or softness, ignoring that diamond is non-metallic and very hard.
misconceptions.fix: Metallic minerals contain metals (iron, copper, bauxite); non-metallic ones (mica, limestone, diamond, coal) do not. Hardness is not what separates the groups.

probe.question: Diamond is the hardest natural substance. Is it a metallic or non-metallic mineral?
probe.wrong_answer: Metallic, because it is very hard.

misconceptions.root_belief: Hardness and strength define metallic minerals

misconceptions.statement: Ferrous minerals are those that contain rust.
misconceptions.why: Students know iron rusts and mix up the word 'ferrous' with the rust that forms on iron.
misconceptions.fix: Ferrous minerals contain iron (iron ore, manganese, nickel, cobalt in steel-making); they are classified by iron content, not by rust. Non-ferrous minerals such as copper, bauxite and lead have no iron in them.

probe.question: Why is iron ore called a ferrous mineral?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it rusts when exposed to air and water.

misconceptions.root_belief: Classification names come from visible properties like rust

misconceptions.statement: Open-cast mining is done only on the surface of the ground by simply picking up minerals, with no machines or blasting.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'open' means shallow and easy, and picture a small surface scraping.
misconceptions.fix: Open-cast mining removes minerals from shallow deposits by digging large open pits, often with blasting, drilling and heavy machines; it is cheaper and quicker than shaft mining, which is used for deep deposits.

probe.question: Which method needs heavy machinery and blasting, open-cast or shaft mining?
probe.wrong_answer: Only shaft mining; open-cast is just picking minerals from the surface.

misconceptions.root_belief: Open surface work means simple, small-scale activity

misconceptions.statement: Mining methods are chosen by the type of mineral, not by how deep the deposit lies.
misconceptions.why: Students link a specific mineral with a specific method and miss the depth factor.
misconceptions.fix: The method depends mainly on the depth and position of the deposit: shallow deposits use open-cast, deep ones use shaft (underground) mining; quarrying is used for stones near the surface.

probe.question: A coal seam lies very close to the surface. Which mining method is likely used?
probe.wrong_answer: Shaft mining, because coal is always mined that way.

misconceptions.root_belief: Each mineral has one fixed mining method

misconceptions.statement: Solar energy is renewable, so solar panels work equally well day and night and in all weather.
misconceptions.why: Students equate 'renewable and inexhaustible' with 'always available', ignoring that the Sun is not available at night or in cloud.
misconceptions.fix: Sunlight is a renewable resource, but the energy a panel gives depends on sunshine hours and weather, so storage (batteries) or other sources are needed at night and in cloudy periods.

probe.question: Can a solar panel alone power a village light all night?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because solar energy never runs out.

misconceptions.root_belief: Renewable means constantly available without limits
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' ideas about renewable energy

misconceptions.statement: Coal is a fossil fuel because it is dug out of the ground like fossils.
misconceptions.why: Students take 'fossil' to mean anything dug from the earth, not its origin from ancient living matter.
misconceptions.fix: Coal is a fossil fuel because it formed over millions of years from plants buried and compressed under heat and pressure. Petroleum and natural gas form from marine organisms.

probe.question: Why is coal called a fossil fuel?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is dug up from underground, like fossils.

misconceptions.root_belief: Fossil fuel means anything extracted from underground
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' ideas about fossil fuels

misconceptions.statement: Conventional energy sources are the ones that are new and modern, while non-conventional ones are old.
misconceptions.why: Students read 'conventional' as 'advanced' rather than 'traditionally used'.
misconceptions.fix: Conventional sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas, firewood, hydel power) have been in common use for long and are mostly exhaustible; non-conventional sources (solar, wind, tidal, biogas, geothermal) are newer and largely renewable.

probe.question: Which is the conventional source: coal or wind energy?
probe.wrong_answer: Wind energy, because it is the modern technology.

misconceptions.statement: Conserving minerals means we should stop using them completely.
misconceptions.why: Students think saving a resource means not using it, instead of using it carefully.
misconceptions.fix: Sustainable use means using minerals and energy wisely: avoiding wastage, recycling metals, using substitutes and efficient technologies, and relying more on renewable sources so future generations also have them.

probe.question: What should we do to conserve mineral resources?
probe.wrong_answer: Stop mining and using them altogether.

misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' conceptions of conservation
